newsitem.title: INDIA: Guns and politicking on Kashmir campaign trail.
newsitem.headline: Guns and politicking on Kashmir campaign trail.

text.p: Shabnam Shafik spent one hour pinned down by gunfire this week. Then he returned to the campaign trail.
Shafik, a militant-turned-politician, is one of 142 candidates contesting Kashmir's first local assembly elections in nearly a decade.
Campaigning for the elections, which start on Sunday, is a mix of old-fashioned slogans and modern weaponry.
"Pro-government gunmen fired on me repeatedly for over an hour," said Shafik, in Sumbal village, north Kashmir, on Thursday. "The government is playing a double game."

Candidates from Shafik's Congress party and the state's largest political grouping, the National Conference, say government-backed militants have attacked their activists and threatened voters. The government denies the charges.
"The fear is tremendous," said former state chief minister Farooq Abdullah, head of the National Conference. "Guns are still around. It is one of the tragedies we have to face."
Authorities say more than 20,000 people have died in insurgency-related violence since a separatist rebellion broke out in 1990 and the state government was dissolved.
Some 200,000 soldiers, police and paramilitary troopers are deployed in Jammu and Kashmir state for voting on Saturday.
Other parts of the Himalayan state will vote on three other days this month in the first assembly polls since 1987.
Dozens of armed militant groups are fighting Indian rule.
Officials say hundreds of insurgents, called renegades, have jumped to militias which separatists claim are linked to security forces. The government has denied the charge.
Shafik, 35, was a constable before the revolt erupted. Then he turned militant. Now he is an aspiring politician wearing a blue blazer and an open-collar shirt.
"People want elections, they want freedom. People have suffered for six years," Shafik said.
All candidates have round-the-clock security, including 10 police guards and paramilitary troopers, and bullet-proof cars.
Abdullah travels with five specially-trained commandos, dressed in black and with machineguns ready.
A rally on a patch of grass outside the Sumbal police station, about 40 km (25 miles) from Srinagar, draws 200 people and about half as many security personnel.
"Long live Farooq Abdullah!" the all-male crowd shouts, punching fists in the air.
"We will counter the gun," Abdullah says, speaking from a makeshift wooden dias with the wooded Himalayan foothills in the background. "You must vote."
A government intelligence agent on the edge of the crowd says the elections are no solution to the violence. "There is not much enthusiasm. This is all drama," he says.
But Syed Ashiq Hussain, a 35-year-old technician at a government hospital, says an elected government can bring peace. "People have been trampled under the tyrant's boots," he said.
Mujahid Mohammad Abdullah, a National Conference candidate in nearby Baramulla town, agrees.
"The gun is no solution to the problem. We want to come to the table for talks," he says.
Mujahid Abdullah, who travels in an armour-plated police car, says three bomb blasts in Baramulla this week have kept voters away from rallies but he is not afraid.
"If somebody kills me, I don't care," he said.
Jodh Singh, a 91-year-old High School headmaster, says he will cast a vote against the "gun culture".
"Militancy is all in vain," he said. "I will cast my vote at any cost. Death is in the hands of God, not the militants."
